strategos.s: Strategos is a Greek word meaning general, used in the Hellenistic world for military and civil governors. In the Seleucid Empire, satrapies were administered by governors called strategoi or satraps.

stuart-munro-hay.s: Stuart Munro-Hay was a British historian and archaeologist who specialised in the history of Aksum and Ethiopia. The Aksumite Empire profile quotes his description of the sixth-century Yemen campaign as Aksum's swan song as a great power.

su-wei.s: Su Wei was a chancellor of the Sui dynasty of China. The Gokturk Empire profile notes that he documented the Chinese strategy of setting the steppe peoples against each other.

subah.s: A subah was a province of the Mughal Empire, governed by a subahdar. The system was formalised under Akbar.

subartu.s: Subartu was an ancient name for a region of northern Mesopotamia. The Babylonian Empire profile lists it among the members of a coalition defeated by Hammurabi.

subedar.s: A subedar was a provincial governor or military officer in India. In the Maratha Empire, provinces were governed by sardars or subedars.

sublime-porte.s: The Sublime Porte was the name given to the central government of the Ottoman Empire, after the gate leading to the grand vizier's offices in Istanbul. The Ottoman Empire profile describes it as the seat of administration.

sub-saharan-africa.s: Sub-Saharan Africa is the part of Africa south of the Sahara. It was linked to North Africa and the Mediterranean by trans-Saharan trade.

subsidy.s: A subsidy is a payment made by a state to support another party. The Byzantine Empire paid subsidies to neighbouring peoples to turn enemies into allies.

subutai.s: Subutai was one of the leading generals of Genghis Khan and his successor Ögedei. He led campaigns across Central Asia, Russia and eastern Europe.

succession-crisis.s: A succession crisis refers to the recurring pattern in which disputes over who should inherit power weakened empires. Lacking clear rules, rival heirs often fought civil wars.

suchet-singh.s: Suchet Singh was one of the Dogra brothers who held powerful positions at the Lahore court of the Sikh Empire. With his brothers Dhian Singh and Gulab Singh, he took part in the court intrigues after Ranjit Singh's death.

sudan.s: Sudan refers both to the modern country on the Nile and, historically, to the bilad al-Sudan, the broad belt of West and Central African savannah south of the Sahara. Arab geographers used the term for the lands of the Ghana, Mali, Songhai and Kanem-Bornu empires.

suez-crisis.s: The Suez Crisis was the international crisis of 1956 in which Britain, France and Israel invaded Egypt after Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal. Under pressure from the United States and the Soviet Union, the invaders withdrew.

suffete.s: A suffete was one of the chief elected magistrates of Carthage and other Phoenician cities. Usually two suffetes held office each year, presiding over the council and the courts.

sufism.s: Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam, which seeks direct personal experience of God through devotion, prayer and spiritual discipline, often within orders led by masters. The Safavid Empire grew out of the Safaviyya Sufi order.

sugar-plantation.s: A sugar plantation is a large agricultural estate growing sugarcane for sugar production, typically using intensive labour. From the fifteenth century such plantations, worked by enslaved Africans, spread from Atlantic islands to Brazil and the Caribbean.

sugarcane.s: Sugarcane is a tall tropical grass whose stalks are crushed to produce sugar. It was cultivated in India since ancient times.

sui-dynasty.s: The Sui dynasty reunified China in 581–589 after centuries of division and ruled until 618. It built the Grand Canal but exhausted the country with costly wars, including campaigns in Korea.

sukkal.s: Sukkal was a title of high office in ancient Elam, originally meaning envoy or minister. In the Sukkalmah period the sukkal of Susa was one of the three leading rulers.

sukkalmah.s: Sukkalmah, meaning grand regent, was the title of the supreme ruler of Elam during the Sukkalmah period. The holder stood at the head of a tripartite hierarchy with the sukkal of Susa and the king of Anshan and Susa.

sukkalmah-period.s: The Sukkalmah period was the era of Elamite history c. 1970–1500 BCE, when Elam was ruled by grand regents called sukkalmahs.

sulawesi.s: Sulawesi is a large island in eastern Indonesia. It was linked to the trading networks of the archipelago.

suleiman-solong.s: Suleiman Solong was the founder of the Darfur Sultanate in the early seventeenth century. According to the Darfur Sultanate profile, he consolidated the authority of the Keira clan over the diverse peoples of the Marrah Mountains region.

suleiman-the-magnificent.s: Suleiman the Magnificent, known in Turkish as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, was Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566. He conquered Belgrade, won the Battle of Mohács, besieged Vienna and extended Ottoman power in the Mediterranean.

suleymaniye-mosque.s: The Süleymaniye Mosque is an imperial mosque in Istanbul built for Suleiman the Magnificent by the architect Mimar Sinan in the 1550s. It is one of the largest and most celebrated works of Ottoman architecture.

sulh-i-kul.s: Sulh-i-kul, meaning peace with all or universal tolerance, was a principle of religious tolerance associated with the Mughal emperor Akbar. It aimed to govern a diverse population of Muslims, Hindus and others without favouring one faith.

sultan.s: Sultan is an Arabic title meaning authority or power, used by Muslim rulers. The Seljuk rulers were among the first to use it as a formal title, alongside the caliph.

sultan-husayn.s: Sultan Husayn, also known as Shah Sultan Husayn, was the Safavid ruler of Iran from 1694 to 1722. His weak rule saw the decline of the state.

sultanate-of-rum.s: The Sultanate of Rum was a Seljuk state in Anatolia from the late eleventh century to the early fourteenth century, with its capital at Konya. It emerged as a branch of the Seljuk dynasty.

sultaniyya.s: Sultaniyya was a city in north-western Iran built as a capital of the Ilkhanate under Öljeitü. Its great domed mausoleum, built around 1313, is a masterpiece of Ilkhanid architecture.

sumanguru-kante.s: Sumanguru Kanté was the ruler of the Sosso Empire in West Africa in the early thirteenth century. He was defeated by Sundiata Keita at the Battle of Kirina around 1235.

sumatra.s: Sumatra is a large island in western Indonesia, lying along the Strait of Malacca. It was the home of Srivijaya, based at Palembang.

sumer.s: Sumer was the region of southern Mesopotamia where one of the world's earliest civilisations developed, with city-states such as Ur, Uruk and Lagash. It was conquered by Sargon of Akkad.

sumerian-king-list.s: The Sumerian King List is an ancient Mesopotamian text listing the kings of Sumer and the cities that held kingship. It mixes legendary and historical rulers.

sumerian-language.s: The Sumerian language was the language of ancient Sumer, one of the earliest written languages. It is unrelated to any known language.

sumpah.s: Sumpah is a Malay word meaning oath. According to the Srivijaya Empire profile, Srivijaya used oaths of loyalty to bind subordinate port polities.

sumptuary-law.s: A sumptuary law is a law that restricts consumption, such as clothing or luxury goods, often according to social rank. The Han Dynasty profile notes that merchants were subject to sumptuary restrictions.

sumuabum.s: Sumuabum was an Amorite chieftain who founded the First Dynasty of Babylon around c. 1894 BCE.

sumu-la-el.s: Sumu-la-El was an early king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, successor to Sumuabum. He was one of the five rulers who preceded Hammurabi.

sunda-strait.s: The Sunda Strait is the channel between Java and Sumatra connecting the Java Sea to the Indian Ocean. The Srivijaya Empire profile notes that Palembang was positioned to control shipping through the Malacca and Sunda straits.

sundiata-keita.s: Sundiata Keita was the founder of the Mali Empire, who died c. 1255.

sunni-ali.s: Sunni Ali was ruler of Songhai from 1464 to 1492 and the founder of the Songhai Empire. He captured Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenné around 1473.

sunni-islam.s: Sunni Islam is the largest branch of Islam, whose followers accept the legitimacy of the first four caliphs. It was the religion of states such as the Umayyad Caliphate, the Seljuk Empire, the Ayyubid Empire and the Ottoman Empire.

sunni-shia-divide.s: The Sunni–Shia divide is the split between the two main branches of Islam, which originated in the dispute over the succession to the Prophet Muhammad. The Rashidun Caliphate profile traces its origins to the succession debate at Saqifah.

suppiluliuma-i.s: Suppiluliuma I was a king of the Hittite Empire who reigned c. 1344–1322 BCE.

surat.s: Surat is a port city in Gujarat in western India, a major commercial centre under the Mughal Empire. In 1664 the Maratha leader Shivaji raided it.

suriname.s: Suriname is a country on the north-eastern coast of South America, formerly a Dutch colony. The Dutch Empire profile notes that Suriname became independent on 25 November 1975.

surrender-of-japan.s: The surrender of Japan was formally signed on 2 September 1945 aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. It ended the Second World War.

suryavarman-ii.s: Suryavarman II was a king of the Khmer Empire in the first half of the twelfth century. He built the temple of Angkor Wat and campaigned against the Cham and other neighbours.

susa.s: Susa was an ancient city in south-western Iran, the capital of Elam and later an Achaemenid royal capital. It was the eastern terminus of the Royal Road and an important Achaemenid administrative centre.

sushruta.s: Sushruta was an ancient Indian physician, the traditional author of a surgical compendium. It described procedures such as rhinoplasty and cataract surgery.

sutlej-river.s: The Sutlej River is a river of the Punjab, a tributary of the Indus. It formed the boundary between the Sikh Empire and British territory.

sveriges-riksbank.s: Sveriges Riksbank is the central bank of Sweden, founded in 1668. It is the oldest central bank still operating.

sviatoslav-i-of-kiev.s: Sviatoslav I of Kiev was a prince of Kievan Rus in the tenth century. In the 960s he campaigned against the Khazars, destroying their power.

sviatoslavs-campaign-against-the-khazars.s: Sviatoslav's campaign against the Khazars was a series of military expeditions by the prince of Kievan Rus in the 960s. He captured Sarkel and other Khazar centres.

swahili.s: The Swahili are a people of the East African coast, whose culture developed through interaction between Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab and Persian traders. Swahili merchants traded gold, ivory and other goods.

swati.s: The Swati, or Swazi, are a Nguni-speaking people of southern Africa. During the Mfecane, Swati forces under Queen Nyamazana invaded the Zimbabwean plateau.

sweden.s: Sweden is a kingdom in northern Europe on the eastern side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In the seventeenth century it became the core of the Swedish Empire, a Baltic great power whose armies intervened decisively in the Thirty Years' War and fought repeatedly against the…

swedish-east-india-company.s: The Swedish East India Company was a chartered trading company founded in 1731 and based in Gothenburg. It traded chiefly with China and South Asia, importing tea, porcelain, silk and other Asian goods into northern European markets.

swedish-empire.s: The Swedish Empire refers to the period, known in Swedish as Stormaktstiden or the Age of Great Power, when Sweden dominated the Baltic region in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. Built on military reform, Baltic conquests and gains from the Thirty Years' War, it…

sweet-potato.s: The sweet potato is a starchy root crop native to the Americas that spread across the world after the sixteenth century through Spanish and Portuguese trade networks. In China it was one of several New World crops, alongside maize and peanuts, that allowed cultivation of…

switzerland.s: Switzerland is a mountainous country in central Europe whose territory formed part of the Holy Roman Empire in the medieval period. The Holy Roman Empire profile lists it among the lands, together with modern Germany, Austria, the Czech lands, northern Italy and the Low…

syncretism.s: Syncretism is the blending of different religious, philosophical or cultural traditions into new combined forms. The Macedonian Empire's conquests fostered a fusion of Greek and Eastern knowledge, while the Roman Empire absorbed foreign deities into its pantheon.

synthetic-dye.s: Synthetic dyes are colourants produced by industrial chemistry rather than extracted from plants or animals, a technology that developed rapidly from the mid-nineteenth century. Firms such as BASF, Bayer and Hoechst made the German Empire the world leader in the field.

syr-darya.s: The Syr Darya is a major river of Central Asia that flows from the Tian Shan mountains north-westwards to the Aral Sea. Known to classical writers as the Jaxartes, it marked an important frontier between the settled lands of Transoxiana and the steppe.

syria.s: Syria is a historical region of the eastern Mediterranean, lying between Anatolia, Mesopotamia, Arabia and Egypt. Its cities, trade routes and fertile lands made it one of the most contested regions in history, fought over by the Hittite, Egyptian, Assyrian, Seleucid,…

syriac.s: Syriac is a dialect of Aramaic that became the main literary and liturgical language of many Christian communities in the Near East from the early centuries CE. Syriac-speaking scholars translated and transmitted Greek philosophy and science.

syrian-wars.s: The Syrian Wars were a series of conflicts fought between the Ptolemaic and Seleucid kingdoms during the third and second centuries BCE. They centred on control of Coele-Syria, the strategically and commercially valuable territory between Egypt and Syria.

szlachta.s: The szlachta was the hereditary noble class of Poland and later of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Unusually numerous, it enjoyed extensive privileges, including the right to elect the king and to participate in the Sejm.

shalmaneser-iii.s: Shalmaneser III was king of Assyria from 859 to 824 BCE. He campaigned almost every year, annexing Bit-Adini on the Euphrates, fighting a coalition of Syrian and Levantine kings at Qarqar in 853 BCE, and taking tribute from Israel, as shown on his Black Obelisk.

santo-domingo.s: Santo Domingo, on the south coast of Hispaniola, was founded by the Spanish in the 1490s and is the oldest continuously inhabited European city in the Americas. It was the seat of the first royal audiencia in the New World and the capital of the Spanish colony.

social-war-91-87-bce.s: The Social War was the revolt of Rome's Italian allies, led by the Marsi and Samnites, who demanded Roman citizenship. It began with the killing of Romans at Asculum in Picenum in 91 BCE.

social-war-357-355-bce.s: The Social War of 357–355 BCE was fought between Athens and members of the Second Athenian League, led by Chios, Rhodes, Kos and Byzantium, with support from Mausolus of Caria. The rebels defeated the Athenian fleet at Embata, and Athens was forced to recognise their…

santa-fe-argentina.s: Santa Fe is a city on the Paraná river in northern Argentina, founded by Juan de Garay in 1573 as a stopping place between Asunción and the Río de la Plata. It belonged to the Governorate of Buenos Aires from 1617.

santa-fe-new-mexico.s: Santa Fe was founded around 1610 by the Spanish governor Pedro de Peralta as the capital of the province of New Mexico, on the northern frontier of New Spain. Pueblo rebels drove the Spanish out in 1680, and Diego de Vargas reoccupied it in 1692.

swabian-circle.s: The Swabian Circle was one of the Imperial Circles into which the Holy Roman Empire was divided from 1500 to organise defence, coinage and peace-keeping. It covered south-western Germany and was the most fragmented of all, with nearly a hundred members, including Württemberg,…

saint-boniface.s: Saint Boniface was an English monk, born Winfrid, who led the papal mission to the Germans. He worked in Thuringia and Hesse, organised the dioceses of Bavaria, among them Passau, Regensburg, Freising and Eichstätt, and founded Würzburg and the abbey of Fulda.

southern-maratha-country.s: The Southern Maratha Country was the British name for the region between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, covering parts of modern southern Maharashtra and northern Karnataka. After the fall of the Peshwa in 1818 its Maratha jagirdars, such as the Patwardhans of Sangli,…

saint-vincent-island.s: Saint Vincent is a volcanic island of the Windward Islands in the Caribbean. It long remained in the hands of the Kalinago and the Garifuna, people of mixed African and Kalinago descent, who resisted European settlement.

santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico.s: Santa Fe de Nuevo México was a province on the northern frontier of New Spain, founded by Juan de Oñate's colonising expedition in 1598, with its capital at Santa Fe from about 1610. The Pueblo Revolt drove the Spanish out from 1680 to 1692.

santa-cruz-massacre.s: The Santa Cruz massacre took place on 12 November 1991, when Indonesian troops opened fire on mourners and pro-independence demonstrators at the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili, East Timor. Estimates of the dead range up to around 250.

simon-bolivar.s: Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan leader of the wars of independence against Spain, known as the Liberator. After the fall of the First and Second Venezuelan republics he regrouped in Jamaica and Haiti, where Alexandre Pétion supplied him in return for a promise to free slaves.

stamford-raffles.s: Thomas Stamford Raffles was a British official of the East India Company. He served at Penang from 1805 and was Lieutenant-Governor of Java from 1811 to 1816 during the British occupation, when he reformed land revenue, deposed or reduced Javanese rulers and wrote a History of…

sir-william-penn.s: Sir William Penn was an English admiral who commanded the fleet of Oliver Cromwell's Western Design against the Spanish Caribbean. With General Robert Venables he failed to take Santo Domingo in 1655 but captured Jamaica instead, beginning English rule of the island.

sigismund-holy-roman-emperor.s: Sigismund of Luxembourg was King of Hungary from 1387, King of the Romans from 1411, King of Bohemia from 1419 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1433. He led the crusade defeated at Nicopolis in 1396 and convened the Council of Constance, which ended the Western Schism and condemned…

swiss-peasant-war-of-1653.s: The Swiss peasant war of 1653 was a revolt of the rural subjects of Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel against their patrician city governments, set off by a devaluation of the currency and falling prices after the Thirty Years' War. Led by Niklaus Leuenberger, the peasants…

sao-luis.s: São Luís is a port city on the island of Maranhão in northern Brazil. It was founded in 1612 by the French as Fort Saint-Louis, centre of Equinoctial France, and taken by the Portuguese in 1615.

shah-jahan.s: Shah Jahan was the fifth Mughal emperor, ruling from 1628 to 1658. His reign marked the height of Mughal architecture, with the Taj Mahal at Agra, built for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and the new capital of Shahjahanabad at Delhi.

shah-mir.s: Shah Mir was the founder of the Shah Mir dynasty and of the Kashmir Sultanate. An immigrant who rose to high office at the Hindu court of Kashmir after the Mongol raid of 1320, he seized power from Queen Kota Rani in 1339 and ruled as Sultan Shams-ud-Din until 1342.

shan-state.s: Shan State is the largest state of Myanmar, covering the Shan Plateau in the east of the country. It was formed in 1948 from the Federated Shan States when Burma became independent, after Shan leaders agreed at the Panglong Conference of 1947 to join the new Union.

stefan-dusan.s: Stefan Dušan was King of Serbia from 1331 and was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks in 1346. He conquered much of Byzantine Macedonia, Albania, Epirus and Thessaly, raised the Serbian church to a patriarchate and issued the law code known as Dušan's Code in 1349.

stefan-lazarevic.s: Stefan Lazarević was the son of Prince Lazar, who fell at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. He ruled Moravian Serbia as an Ottoman vassal and fought for the sultan at Ankara in 1402, after which Byzantium granted him the title of despot.

suez-canal.s: The Suez Canal is a sea-level waterway across the Isthmus of Suez in Egypt, linking the Mediterranean with the Red Sea. Built by a French-led company under a concession granted by Said Pasha in 1854, it opened in 1869 and transformed the route between Europe and Asia, raising…

sun-yat-sen.s: Sun Yat-sen was a Chinese revolutionary and founder of the Kuomintang (Nationalist Party). After the 1911 revolution he became provisional president of the Republic of China in January 1912 but soon gave way to Yuan Shikai.

sunan-gunung-jati.s: Sunan Gunung Jati was one of the Wali Songo, the Nine Saints credited with spreading Islam in Java. He is regarded as the founder of the Cirebon Sultanate and, with his son Maulana Hasanuddin, led the forces of Demak and Cirebon that took Banten from the Sunda Kingdom around…

san-francisco.s: San Francisco is a port city on the Pacific coast of California, founded as a Spanish presidio and mission in 1776. It passed to Mexico and then, in 1848, to the United States, and the California gold rush turned it into the main city of the American West.

san-juan-puerto-rico.s: San Juan is the capital of Puerto Rico, on a bay on the island's north coast. Spanish settlers moved there from Caparra around 1521, and it grew into a heavily fortified port guarding the routes of the Spanish treasure fleets, with the fortress of El Morro.

santiago-del-estero.s: Santiago del Estero is a city in north-western Argentina, founded by the Spanish in 1553 and the oldest surviving Spanish town in the country. It was the first seat of the Governorate of Tucumán and the base for founding other towns in the region.

seretse-khama.s: Seretse Khama was the hereditary chief of the Bangwato and the first President of Botswana, from 1966 until his death in 1980. His marriage to an Englishwoman, Ruth Williams, led Britain to exile him from the Bechuanaland Protectorate in the 1950s.

shi-le.s: Shi Le was a Jie warlord who rose from slavery to become a general of the Han-Zhao state, helping to capture the Jin capital Luoyang in 311. In 319 he broke away and founded the Later Zhao, and in 329 he destroyed Former Zhao, making Later Zhao the strongest state in northern…

sho-hashi.s: Shō Hashi was the unifier of Okinawa and first king of the unified Ryukyu Kingdom. He seized Chūzan in 1406, installing his father as king, conquered Hokuzan in 1416 and Nanzan in 1429, bringing the three kingdoms under one ruler.

sierra-morena.s: The Sierra Morena is a mountain range in southern Spain separating the central plateau from the Guadalquivir valley. Rich in silver, lead and copper, its mines were worked by Iberian peoples and later by Carthage and Rome, and towns such as Castulo grew wealthy from them.

simla-hill-states.s: The Simla Hill States were a group of small princely states in the western Himalayan foothills around Shimla, most of them ruled by Rajput families. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814–1816 they came under British protection, supervised by a superintendent at Shimla.

sisavang-vong.s: Sisavang Vong was King of Luang Phrabang from 1904 under French protection and King of Laos from 1946 until his death in 1959. In 1945 he sided with France against the Lao Issara movement of Prince Phetsarath, and under him Laos became a constitutional monarchy within the…

sobhuza-ii.s: Sobhuza II was King of Swaziland from 1899, ruling in person from 1921 until his death in 1982, one of the longest recorded reigns. He campaigned for the return of land lost to concessions under British rule and led the country to independence in 1968.

state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.n: State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.s: The State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs was a short-lived state proclaimed in Zagreb in October 1918 by the South Slav lands leaving Austria-Hungary. Governed by a national council, it united Slovenia, Croatia-Slavonia, Dalmatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina.

stefan-nemanja.s: Stefan Nemanja was Grand Prince of Serbia from about 1166 to 1196 and founder of the Nemanjić dynasty. He united the Serbian lands, conquering Duklja and Zachlumia, and won independence from Byzantium in practice.

swabian-league.s: The Swabian League was an alliance of princes, knights and imperial cities in south-western Germany, founded at Esslingen in 1488 with the backing of Emperor Frederick III to keep the peace and resist Bavarian expansion. Its army expelled Duke Ulrich of Württemberg in 1519 and…

syngman-rhee.s: Syngman Rhee was a Korean independence activist and the first President of South Korea, from 1948 to 1960. He was the first president of the Korean Provisional Government in exile in 1919, spent decades in the United States, and returned in 1945 with American support.

syriac-christians.s: Syriac Christians are the Christian communities of the Middle East whose liturgy and literature use Syriac, a form of Aramaic. They include the Syriac Orthodox Church, the Church of the East and the Maronites.

southern-cameroons.s: The Southern Cameroons was the southern part of the British Cameroons, a mandated and later trust territory administered with Nigeria, with Buea as its centre. It gained its own government in the 1950s.

sabit-damulla.s: Sabit Damulla was a Uyghur Islamic scholar and nationalist from Atush who became prime minister of the First East Turkestan Republic, proclaimed at Kashgar in November 1933. The republic sought an Islamic state independent of China.

saint-croix.s: Saint Croix is the largest of the United States Virgin Islands. It was contested by the Dutch, English and Spanish before France took it in 1650; the Knights of Malta held it briefly from 1651 to 1665.

salih-ibn-mirdas.s: Salih ibn Mirdas was an emir of the Banu Kilab Arabs who founded the Mirdasid dynasty. In 1024 he captured Aleppo from the Fatimid governor, ending the rule of the Lu'lu'id regents, and held much of northern Syria.

sancho-iii-of-navarre.s: Sancho III, called the Great, was king of Pamplona (Navarre) from about 1004 to 1035 and the most powerful ruler of Christian Spain. He brought Sobrarbe and Ribagorza under his control, dominated Castile through marriage and held León for a time.

sanhaja.s: The Sanhaja were one of the great Berber confederations of the medieval Maghreb, alongside the Zenata and the Masmuda. Their branches included the Zirids of Ifriqiya and Granada and the Hammadids in the central Maghreb, while their Saharan veiled branch, the Lamtuna, founded…

saparmurat-niyazov.s: Saparmurat Niyazov was first secretary of the Communist Party of the Turkmen SSR from 1985 and president of independent Turkmenistan from 1991 until his death in 2006. Styling himself Turkmenbashi, "head of the Turkmen", he built an extreme personality cult, renamed months…

sayf-al-dawla.s: Sayf al-Dawla was a Hamdanid prince who founded the Emirate of Aleppo in 945, while his brother Nasir al-Dawla held Mosul. He waged constant war on the Byzantine frontier with early success, though Nikephoros Phokas sacked Aleppo in 962.

sayyida-al-hurra.s: Sayyida al-Hurra was a Muslim noblewoman from a family of Granada refugees, daughter of the founder of Chefchaouen. After the death of her husband al-Mandri she governed Tetouan from about 1515 to 1542 and directed corsair raids against Spain and Portugal, allied with the…

second-crusade.s: The Second Crusade was launched after the Zengid capture of Edessa in 1144, ending the County of Edessa's capital. Preached by Bernard of Clairvaux, it was led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany, both of whose armies suffered heavy losses in Anatolia.

second-peace-of-thorn.s: The Second Peace of Thorn, signed at Toruń in October 1466, ended the Thirteen Years' War between the Teutonic Order and Poland. Western Prussia, with Danzig and the Order's former capital Marienburg, became Royal Prussia under the Polish crown, together with the bishopric of…

seru-epenisa-cakobau.s: Seru Epenisa Cakobau was the paramount chief of Bau, a small island state off Viti Levu that dominated much of Fiji in the mid-19th century. He converted to Christianity in 1854, and in 1871 he became king of a united Kingdom of Fiji.

seven-sages-of-the-bamboo-grove.n: Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove
seven-sages-of-the-bamboo-grove.s: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove were a group of Chinese scholars and poets of the 3rd century, among them Ji Kang and Ruan Ji. They were known for drinking, music and philosophical "pure conversation" drawing on Daoist thought, and for avoiding service at a dangerous court.

seven-sages-of-greece.s: The Seven Sages of Greece were statesmen and philosophers of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE honoured in Greek tradition for their wisdom and maxims. Lists varied, but usually included Thales of Miletus, Solon of Athens, Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mytilene and Cleobulus of Lindos.

shi-jingtang.s: Shi Jingtang was a Shatuo general and son-in-law of Emperor Mingzong of the Later Tang. In 936 he rebelled at Taiyuan and, with the help of the Khitan Liao dynasty, overthrew the Later Tang and founded the Later Jin.

shibata-katsuie.s: Shibata Katsuie was a senior general of Oda Nobunaga. He conquered Echizen and Kaga, crushing the Ikko-ikki of Kaga in 1580, and ruled from Kitanosho castle at modern Fukui.

sima-ang.s: Sima Ang was a general of the state of Zhao who joined the rising against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Yin, with lands around the old Shang capital in northern Henan.

sima-xin.s: Sima Xin was a Qin officer who surrendered with Zhang Han to Xiang Yu in 207 BCE. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Sai, one of the three kingdoms carved from the Qin homeland.

sinan-pasha-ottoman-admiral.s: Sinan Pasha was Kapudan Pasha, grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet, from about 1550 to 1554 and a brother of the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha. In August 1551, together with the corsair Turgut Reis, he besieged Tripoli and forced the Knights Hospitaller to surrender it, bringing…

sixteen-prefectures.s: The Sixteen Prefectures were a frontier region of northern China, around modern Beijing and Datong, ceded to the Khitan Liao dynasty by Shi Jingtang in 938 in return for help in founding the Later Jin. The Later Zhou recovered two prefectures in 959, but the rest stayed…

south-carolina.s: South Carolina is a region of the south-eastern United States between the Savannah River and North Carolina. It was home to Mississippian chiefdoms such as Cofitachequi and saw a short-lived French fort at Charlesfort in 1562.

souvanna-phouma.s: Prince Souvanna Phouma was a Lao statesman of the royal family. A member of the Lao Issara nationalist government in 1945, he later served several times as prime minister of the Kingdom of Laos between 1951 and 1975, seeking neutrality and coalition with the Pathet Lao, led by…

st-georges-grenada.s: St. George's is the capital of Grenada, on a harbour on the island's south-west coast.

stefan-dragutin.s: Stefan Dragutin was king of Serbia from 1276 to 1282, when a riding accident led him to hand power to his brother Stefan Milutin. Married to a Hungarian princess, he received the Banate of Mačva and Belgrade from the Hungarian crown in 1284 and ruled the northern lands as a…

stephen-bathory.s: Stephen Báthory was prince of Transylvania from 1571 and king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania from 1576 until his death. A gifted commander, he defeated Ivan IV of Russia in the Livonian War, besieging Pskov, and by the Truce of Yam-Zapolsky in 1582 secured Livonia for…

subhi-barakat.s: Subhi Barakat was a Syrian politician from Antioch who led the Syrian Federation created by the French mandate authorities in 1922. When the federation was replaced by the State of Syria in 1925, he became its head of state, but resigned in 1925 during the Great Syrian Revolt.

sun-quan.s: Sun Quan was the founder of the state of Eastern Wu in southern China during the Three Kingdoms period. Allied with Liu Bei, he defeated Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208, then turned on Shu Han, taking Jing province in 219 and defeating Liu Bei at Xiaoting in 222.

sunan-giri.s: Sunan Giri, born Raden Paku, was one of the Wali Songo, the nine saints credited with spreading Islam in Java. He founded a religious school on the hills of Giri near Gresik in East Java in the late 15th century.

sunda-kelapa.s: Sunda Kelapa was the main port of the Hindu Sunda Kingdom of West Java, at the mouth of the Ciliwung river, exporting pepper. The Portuguese signed a treaty there in 1522, but in 1527 forces of Demak and Cirebon under Fatahillah captured it and renamed it Jayakarta.

supreme-council-of-the-irish-confederati.n: Supreme Council of the Irish Confederation
supreme-council-of-the-irish-confederati.s: The Supreme Council was the executive of Confederate Ireland, the Catholic government set up at Kilkenny in 1642 during the Irish Confederate Wars. Chosen by the General Assembly, it raised armies, levied taxes and negotiated with Charles I and the papal nuncio Rinuccini.

supreme-council-of-the-republic-of-lithu.n: Supreme Council of the Republic of Lithuania
supreme-council-of-the-republic-of-lithu.s: The Supreme Council of Lithuania was the parliament elected in February 1990 with a majority for the Sąjūdis movement, under Vytautas Landsbergis as chairman. On 11 March 1990 it declared the restoration of Lithuania's independence, the first Soviet republic to do so.

supreme-council-of-the-republic-of-latvi.n: Supreme Council of the Republic of Latvia
supreme-council-of-the-republic-of-latvi.s: The Supreme Council of Latvia was the parliament elected in March 1990, in which the Popular Front of Latvia won a majority. On 4 May 1990, under its chairman Anatolijs Gorbunovs, it declared the restoration of Latvia's independence with a transition period, completed on 21…

suro-of-geumgwan-gaya.s: Suro is the legendary founder of Geumgwan Gaya, the leading state of the Gaya confederacy in southern Korea, near modern Gimhae. According to tradition he hatched from a golden egg sent from heaven in 42 CE and married Heo Hwang-ok, a princess from a distant land.

sveinn-bjornsson.s: Sveinn Björnsson was an Icelandic diplomat and statesman. After the German occupation of Denmark in 1940 cut Iceland off from its king, the Althing elected him regent in 1941.

swabian-jura.s: The Swabian Jura, or Swabian Alb, is a limestone upland in south-western Germany, running about 200 km from the Black Forest to the Ries crater. Its steep northern edge was crowned by medieval castles such as Hohenzollern, Teck and Helfenstein, seats of noble families, while…

shahverdi-khan-khorshidi.s: Shahverdi Khan was the last atabeg of the Khorshidi dynasty, which ruled Lesser Luristan in western Iran from the fortress of Falak-ol-Aflak at Khorramabad. After he rebelled against the Safavid shah Abbas I, he was captured and executed in 1597, and Luristan was given to…

state-of-qin.s: The State of Qin was a Zhou-era state in the Wei River valley of western China. After the reforms of Shang Yang in the 4th century BCE it became the strongest military power of the Warring States, conquering Shu in 316 BCE and ending the Zhou royal line in 256 BCE.

swiss-federal-council.s: The Swiss Federal Council is the seven-member executive of the Swiss Confederation, created by the federal constitution of 1848. Its members are elected by the Federal Assembly and govern collectively, each heading a department, with a president who rotates every year.

sigismund-of-burgundy.s: Sigismund of Burgundy was king of the Burgundians from 516 to 524. A convert from Arianism to Catholic Christianity, he founded the abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune.

sigismund-i-the-old.s: Sigismund I the Old was king of Poland and grand duke of Lithuania from 1506 to 1548. By the Treaty of Kraków in 1525 he accepted the homage of his nephew Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who secularised the Teutonic Order's lands as the Duchy of Prussia under Polish overlordship.

sultan-suriansyah.s: Sultan Suriansyah, born Raden Samudra, was the founder of the Banjar Sultanate in southern Borneo. A grandson of the king of Negara Daha, he fled to the coast when his uncle seized the throne.

safar-pasha.s: Safar Pasha was a member of the Georgian Jaqeli family of Samtskhe who converted to Islam and became the first governor of the Ottoman Childir Eyalet when the principality was made a province in 1628. The governorship, based at Akhaltsikhe, remained largely hereditary in his…

said-bin-taimur.s: Said bin Taimur was sultan of Muscat and Oman from 1932 to 1970. He kept the country isolated and frugal, won the Jebel Akhdar War against the Imamate of Oman with British help and sold Gwadar to Pakistan in 1958.

saint-kitts.s: Saint Kitts, formally Saint Christopher, is a Caribbean island in the Leeward Islands. Thomas Warner founded the first English colony in the Caribbean there in 1623, and the French settled in 1625; the two partitioned the island in 1627.

saint-john-us-virgin-islands.s: Saint John is one of the three main islands of the United States Virgin Islands. Settled by Denmark in 1718, it became part of the Danish West Indies, and an uprising of enslaved Africans broke out there in 1733.

saint-john-river.s: The Saint John River flows from Maine through New Brunswick to the Bay of Fundy. About 14,000 Loyalists settled along it after the American Revolution, leading to the creation of the Colony of New Brunswick in 1784, with Fredericton on the river as capital and the city of…

salchak-toka.s: Salchak Toka was the leader of the Tuvan People's Revolutionary Party from 1932. He ran a Stalinist regime in the Tuvan People's Republic, collectivising herds, closing monasteries and persecuting lamas, and oversaw Tuva's annexation by the Soviet Union in 1944.

salvador-correia-de-sa-e-benevides.n: Salvador Correia de Sá e Benevides
salvador-correia-de-sa-e-benevides.s: Salvador Correia de Sá e Benevides was a Portuguese-Brazilian soldier and administrator from a leading Rio de Janeiro family, several times governor of Rio. In 1648 he led a fleet from Brazil that retook Luanda from the Dutch West India Company, restoring Portuguese Angola and…

samnite-wars.s: The Samnite Wars were three wars fought between the Roman Republic and the Samnites of the southern Apennines between 343 and 290 BCE. Despite defeats such as the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE, Rome prevailed and, after the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE, became the dominant power…

samudera-pasai-sultanate.s: The Samudera Pasai Sultanate was a Muslim port kingdom on the north coast of Sumatra, near modern Lhokseumawe, from the late 13th century. Its first known sultan, Malik al-Salih, died in 1297, making it one of the earliest Islamic states in maritime South-East Asia; Ibn…

san-antonio.s: San Antonio is a city in south-central Texas founded by the Spanish in 1718 as a mission and presidio on the San Antonio River. It became the chief settlement and from 1772 the capital of Spanish Texas, and its Mission San Antonio de Valero, the Alamo, was besieged in 1836…

san-salvador.s: San Salvador is the capital of El Salvador, founded by the Spanish in 1525 and re-established in 1528 after Pipil resistance. A provincial capital within the Captaincy General of Guatemala, it became in 1834 the seat of the Federal Republic of Central America, whose liberal…

sancho-ramirez.s: Sancho Ramírez was King of Aragon from 1063 and of Pamplona (Navarre) from 1076 until his death in 1094, the son of Ramiro I. He placed Aragon under papal protection, introduced the Roman liturgy and pushed the frontier south against the taifas of al-Andalus.

sanford-b-dole.s: Sanford B. Dole was a Hawaiian-born lawyer of American missionary parents who led the government formed after the overthrow of Queen Liliuokalani in 1893.

sao-boso.s: Sao Boso, known to Europeans as King Boatswain, was a Mandingo warrior and trader who in the early 19th century built the Condo Confederation around Bopolu in the hinterland of north-western Liberia. Allied with Muslim Mandingo merchants, he controlled trade routes between the…

sao-shwe-thaike.s: Sao Shwe Thaike was the saopha of Yawnghwe, a Shan state on Inle Lake, and the first President of the Union of Burma from 1948 to 1952. A leading figure among the Shan princes at the Panglong Conference of 1947, he helped bring the Shan states into the union.

satake-yoshinobu.s: Satake Yoshinobu was a Japanese daimyo who headed the Satake clan of Hitachi province, one of the largest domains in eastern Japan. Because he stayed neutral at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu moved him in 1602 to Akita in Dewa province with a reduced income,…

saw-yun.s: Saw Yun was the founder of the Sagaing Kingdom in Upper Burma. A son of Thihathu, ruler of Pinya, he quarrelled with his father and in 1315 set up his own court at Sagaing, across the Irrawaddy, which became a rival to Pinya for half a century.

schmalkaldic-league.s: The Schmalkaldic League was a defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and imperial cities of the Holy Roman Empire, founded at Schmalkalden in 1531 and led by Philip of Hesse and John Frederick of Saxony. It resisted Emperor Charles V's efforts to restore Catholic unity until…

sea-of-azov.s: The Sea of Azov is a shallow inland sea north of the Black Sea, linked to it by the Kerch Strait and fed by the Don and Kuban rivers. Its shores and the surrounding steppe were home to successive nomadic peoples, among them the Bulgar Onogurs and Utigurs, and were later…

seku-wattara.s: Seku Wattara was a Dyula Muslim warlord who seized power in the market town of Kong, in present-day northern Ivory Coast, around 1710 and founded the Kong Empire. His campaigns extended Kong's influence north towards the Black Volta and the middle Niger, protecting caravan…

senusret-iii.s: Senusret III was a pharaoh of the Twelfth Dynasty of Middle Kingdom Egypt, reigning in the 19th century BCE. He curbed the power of the provincial nomarchs and campaigned repeatedly in Nubia, strengthening the fortresses around the Second Cataract such as Semna.

sergio-osmena.s: Sergio Osmeña was a Filipino politician who, with Manuel Quezon, led the Nacionalista Party and campaigned for independence under American rule, helping to secure the Tydings–McDuffie Act of 1934. He became vice-president of the Commonwealth of the Philippines in 1935 and…

servius-tullius.s: Servius Tullius was, according to Roman tradition, the sixth king of Rome, reigning in the 6th century BCE. He was credited with the first census, the division of citizens into wealth classes that formed the basis of the army and the centuriate assembly, and the so-called…

seuthes-iii.s: Seuthes III was a king of the Odrysian Kingdom in Thrace in the late 4th century BCE. He resisted Lysimachus, Alexander's successor in Thrace, but eventually accepted his overlordship.

shah-ali-khan.s: Shah Ali was a Chinggisid prince of the Qasim Khanate who served the grand princes of Moscow. Moscow installed him as Khan of Kazan three times, in 1518–1521, 1546 and 1551–1552, but Kazan's nobles rejected him each time; he later led Russian troops in the Livonian War.

shah-husain-arghun.s: Shah Husain Arghun was ruler of Sindh from 1524 to 1556, son of Shah Beg, founder of the Arghun dynasty. He extended Arghun control over lower Sindh around Thatta and in the 1520s took Multan from the Langah Sultanate.

shah-murad.s: Shah Murad was the first emir of Bukhara of the Manghit dynasty, ruling from 1785 until his death in 1800. A pious ruler known for his ascetic life, he set aside the Janid figurehead khans and took the Islamic title of emir.

shah-shuja-durrani.s: Shah Shuja Durrani was a ruler of the Durrani Empire, reigning from 1803 to 1809 and again from 1839 to 1842. Driven out by his brother Shah Mahmud and the Barakzai chiefs, he lived for decades in exile in British India.

shah-shuja-muzaffarid.s: Shah Shuja was ruler of the Muzaffarid dynasty in southern Iran from 1358 to 1384, after deposing and blinding his father Mubariz al-Din Muhammad. His court at Shiraz was a centre of Persian culture, where the poet Hafez enjoyed his favour.

shammar-yahrish.s: Shammar Yahrish was a king of Himyar in south Arabia in the late 3rd and early 4th centuries CE. He absorbed the Kingdom of Saba around 275 and conquered the Kingdom of Hadramawt around 300, uniting south Arabia under Himyarite rule for the first time.

shatuo.s: The Shatuo were a Turkic people of the Western Turkic tradition who settled on the northern frontier of Tang China in the 9th century. Their chief Li Keyong helped the Tang retake Chang'an from Huang Chao in 883 and was rewarded with Hedong, around Taiyuan.

sheikh-hasina.s: Sheikh Hasina is a Bangladeshi politician, daughter of the founding leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and leader of the Awami League. She was prime minister from 1996 to 2001 and again from 2009 to 2024, the country's longest-serving head of government, a period of fast economic…

shen-yang.s: Shen Yang was a former official of Zhao and associate of Zhang Er who, in Xiang Yu's division of the empire in 206 BCE, was made King of Henan, with his capital at Luoyang, as a reward for welcoming Chu forces at the Yellow River. When Liu Bang advanced east in 205 BCE, Shen…

sher-shah-suri.s: Sher Shah Suri was an Afghan ruler who founded the Sur Empire in northern India. After defeating the Mughal emperor Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and Kannauj in 1540, he ruled from Delhi until he was killed at the siege of Kalinjar in 1545.

shi-chaoyi.s: Shi Chaoyi was the last ruler of the rebel Yan state of the An Lushan Rebellion against the Tang dynasty. He had his father Shi Siming killed in 761 and took the throne, but lost Luoyang to Tang and Uyghur forces in 762.

shi-hu.s: Shi Hu was emperor of the Later Zhao, a state of the Jie people in northern China, from 334 to 349. A nephew of the founder Shi Le, he seized power from Shi Le's son, moved the capital to Ye and built lavish palaces with heavy labour levies, earning a reputation for cruelty.

shire-highlands.s: The Shire Highlands are an upland region of southern Malawi, east of the Shire River, around Blantyre and Zomba. Scottish missionaries and traders settled there from the 1870s, and in 1889 Britain declared a protectorate over the area to block Portuguese claims, the core of…

sho-tai.s: Sho Tai was the last king of the Ryukyu Kingdom, reigning from 1848 to 1879. Meiji Japan made him lord of the Ryukyu Domain in 1872 and, when the domain was abolished and annexed as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879, removed him to Tokyo, where he was made a marquis in the Japanese…

siddhi-narasimha-malla.s: Siddhi Narasimha Malla was a Malla king of Lalitpur (Patan) in the Kathmandu Valley, ruling from about 1620 until 1661 as head of a separate kingdom alongside Kantipur and Bhaktapur. Known for his piety, he built the stone Krishna Mandir in Patan Durbar Square, completed in…

sidray-ibn-wazir.s: Sidray ibn Wazir was a commander of the Banu Wazir family in the west of al-Andalus who, in the revolt against the Almoravids in 1144, took Beja and Évora and ruled them as a taifa. His kinsmen took Badajoz in 1145.

simeon-saxe-coburg-gotha.s: Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, as Simeon II, was the last tsar of Bulgaria, succeeding his father Boris III as a child in 1943 under a regency. After the referendum of 1946 abolished the monarchy he went into exile, living mainly in Spain.

simon-vratsian.s: Simon Vratsian was an Armenian Revolutionary Federation politician and the last prime minister of the First Republic of Armenia, taking office in November 1920 as Turkish and Red armies closed in. After the Soviet takeover he joined the rising of 1921 and the Republic of…

sir-harry-smith-1st-baronet.s: Sir Harry Smith was a British army officer who served in the Peninsular War and won the Battle of Aliwal in the First Anglo-Sikh War. As Governor of the Cape Colony from 1847 to 1852 he annexed British Kaffraria between the Keiskamma and Kei rivers and proclaimed the Orange…

sirimavo-bandaranaike.s: Sirimavo Bandaranaike was a Sri Lankan politician who in 1960 became the world's first woman prime minister, leading the Sri Lanka Freedom Party after the assassination of her husband, S. W.

slobodan-milosevic.s: Slobodan Milošević was a Serbian politician who rose through the League of Communists to become president of Serbia from 1989 and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1997 to 2000. His Serbian nationalist policies contributed to the break-up of Yugoslavia and the wars in…

smim-htaw.s: Smim Htaw was the king chosen at Pegu in 1740 by the Mon and other rebels of Lower Burma who rose against the Toungoo dynasty of Ava, reviving the name of the Hanthawaddy kingdom. A former monk, he proved a weak ruler and was replaced in 1747 by Binnya Dala, who went on to…

son-ngoc-thanh.s: Son Ngoc Thanh was a Cambodian nationalist who co-founded the Khmer-language newspaper Nagaravatta in 1936 and fled to Japan in 1942. Back in 1945, he became foreign minister and in August prime minister of the Japanese-sponsored Kingdom of Kampuchea, but the returning French…

songtsen-gampo.s: Songtsen Gampo was the emperor who built the Tibetan Empire in the early 7th century, ruling until 649 with Lhasa as his capital. He conquered Zhangzhung in western Tibet, married princesses from Tang China and, by tradition, Nepal, and is credited with introducing Buddhism…

southern-bug.s: The Southern Bug is a river of Ukraine that flows about 800 km south-east from Podolia to the Black Sea, entering the Dnieper–Bug estuary near Mykolaiv. Known to the Greeks as the Hypanis, it gave the Milesian colony of Olbia on its estuary access to the steppe.

sri-baduga-maharaja.s: Sri Baduga Maharaja, born Jayadewata, was king of Sunda in western Java from 1482 to 1521. He united the crowns of Galuh and Sunda and ruled from Pakuan Pajajaran, near modern Bogor, a period later remembered as Sunda's golden age.

st-augustine-florida.s: St. Augustine is a city on the Atlantic coast of north-east Florida, founded in 1565 by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, who went on to destroy the French Huguenot colony at Fort Caroline.

st-john-river-liberia.s: The St. John River is a river of Liberia that rises in the Nimba highlands of Guinea and flows south-west to the Atlantic at Buchanan.

st-johns-antigua-and-barbuda.s: St. John's is the capital and main port of Antigua, on the island's north-west coast.

st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador.s: St. John's is a port city on the east coast of Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, one of the oldest English settlements in North America and a base of the English cod fishery.

saint-thomas-u-s-virgin-islands.s: Saint Thomas is an island of the U.S. Virgin Islands in the Caribbean, settled by the Danish West India Company in 1672.

stanislaw-leszczynski.s: Stanisław Leszczyński was a Polish noble twice made King of Poland, first in 1704 under Swedish protection during the Great Northern War and again in 1733, when Russian and Austrian intervention in the War of the Polish Succession drove him out. His daughter Marie married…

stefan-the-first-crowned.s: Stefan the First-Crowned was the son of Stefan Nemanja and ruler of Serbia from 1196 to 1228. He was crowned king in 1217 with a crown sent by Pope Honorius III, raising Serbia to a kingdom, while his brother Saint Sava won an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219.

stephen-the-great.s: Stephen the Great was Prince of Moldavia from 1457 to 1504, the principality's outstanding ruler. He defeated an Ottoman army at Vaslui in 1475 and fought Hungary and Poland to defend Moldavian independence, though late in his reign he accepted paying tribute to the Ottomans.

stjepan-vukcic-kosaca.s: Stjepan Vukčić Kosača was the most powerful noble of the Kingdom of Bosnia in the mid-15th century, inheriting Hum and the coast from his uncle Sandalj Hranić in 1435. Often at odds with the Bosnian kings and Ragusa, in 1448 he took the title Herceg of Saint Sava, from which…

sudarshan-shah.s: Sudarshan Shah was the ruler of Garhwal who regained part of his family's kingdom after the Anglo-Nepalese War. His father Pradyumna Shah had been killed fighting the Gorkhas in 1804; in 1815 the British restored Sudarshan Shah to the western part of Garhwal, keeping the east…

sulayman-bal.s: Sulayman Bal was a Fulbe Muslim cleric of Futa Toro in the middle Senegal valley who led the Torodbe clerical movement against the Denianke kings and the Moorish raiders who exacted tribute from the region. He began the revolution in the late 1760s but died in battle around…

suleyman-pasha-candarid.s: Süleyman Pasha was a ruler of the Candarid beylik in northern Anatolia in the early 14th century, son of its founder Şemseddin Yaman Candar. In 1309 he killed the last Chobanid ruler and took Kastamonu, which became the Candarid capital, and around 1322 he added the Black Sea…

sultan-agung.s: Sultan Agung was the third ruler of the Mataram Sultanate in central Java, reigning from 1613 to 1645. He conquered most of Java's north coast, besieging Surabaya until its fall in 1625 and subduing Sumedang, Giri and Madura, and twice besieged Dutch Batavia, in 1628 and 1629,…

sultan-ibn-saif.s: Sultan ibn Saif was imam of Oman of the Ya'aruba dynasty from 1649 to 1688. In 1650 he captured Muscat, ending Portuguese rule on the Omani coast, and built a navy that attacked Portuguese posts in India and East Africa, beginning Oman's rise as a maritime power.

sun-hao.s: Sun Hao was the last emperor of Eastern Wu, one of the Three Kingdoms of China, reigning from 264 to 280. Notorious for cruelty and extravagance, he executed officials and weakened the state.

surat-agency.s: The Surat Agency was a political agency of British India that supervised a group of small princely states in southern Gujarat, among them Dharampur, Bansda and Sachin, through a British political agent based at Surat. Its states were later grouped in the Gujarat States Agency,…

second-white-terror.s: The Second White Terror was a wave of royalist reprisals in southern France in 1815, after Napoleon's Hundred Days and the second restoration of Louis XVIII. Royalist mobs and bands killed Bonapartists, Protestants and former revolutionaries, notably in Marseille, Nîmes and…

state-of-vietnam.s: The State of Vietnam was the French-backed government of Vietnam headed by the former emperor Bảo Đại, created by the Élysée Accords of 1949 as an alternative to Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh. Highland territories such as the Tai Federation were nominally attached to it.

shoshenq-i.s: Shoshenq I was a chief of the Libyan Meshwesh who became pharaoh around 943 BCE and founded the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt, succeeding Psusennes II peacefully. He reunified Egypt by installing his son Iuput as High Priest of Amun at Thebes, ending the independent Theban…

synesius.s: Synesius was a Greek philosopher from Cyrene, a pupil of Hypatia in Alexandria, who became Bishop of Ptolemais in Cyrenaica around 410. His letters and speeches describe the decline of the province, the weakness of its Roman garrison and the raids of desert peoples such as the…

stephen-ii-duke-of-bavaria.s: Stephen II, Duke of Bavaria, was a son of Emperor Louis IV the Bavarian who ruled Lower Bavaria and from 1363 also Upper Bavaria. He reunited much of the Wittelsbach duchy and acquired claims to Tyrol.

stephen-ii-of-naples.s: Stephen II of Naples was duke of Naples from 755 and later also its bishop. Ruling with little reference to the Byzantine emperor, he made the duchy effectively independent, defended it against the Lombards of Benevento and supported the papacy.

shun-emperor.s: Shun is a legendary sage-king of early China, said to have been chosen by Emperor Yao for his virtue and filial piety and to have passed the throne to Yu the Great. Confucian tradition held him up as a model ruler.

sao-luis-maranhao.s: São Luís is the capital of the Brazilian state of Maranhão, on an island off Brazil's northern coast. It grew from Fort Saint-Louis, built in 1612 by the French colonists of Equinoctial France and named after Louis XIII.

sultanate-of-gowa.s: The Sultanate of Gowa was a Makassarese state in south-western Sulawesi, Indonesia, centred on the port of Makassar. Its rulers adopted Islam in 1605 and spread it by alliance and war to neighbouring Bugis lands and to Sumbawa and Bima.

sinjar-mountains.s: The Sinjar Mountains are a ridge rising from the plain of northern Iraq, west of Mosul, near the Syrian border. In the early second millennium BCE the plains around it were home to small kingdoms such as Andarig and Karana, known from the Mari letters and the archives of Tell…

sino-british-joint-declaration.s: The Sino-British Joint Declaration was signed in Beijing on 19 December 1984 by Margaret Thatcher and Zhao Ziyang. Prompted by the expiry of the New Territories lease in 1997, it provided for the transfer of all of Hong Kong to the People's Republic of China on 1 July 1997,…

sino-portuguese-joint-declaration.s: The Sino-Portuguese Joint Declaration was signed in Beijing on 13 April 1987 by Portugal and the People's Republic of China. Following the model of the Hong Kong agreement, it arranged the return of Macau to China on 20 December 1999 as a Special Administrative Region, with…

savang-vatthana.s: Savang Vatthana was the last King of Laos, succeeding his father Sisavang Vong in 1959. His reign coincided with civil war between the royal government and the communist Pathet Lao, and with heavy American bombing.

silko.s: Silko was a king of Nobadia in Lower Nubia known from a Greek inscription in the temple at Kalabsha. In it he calls himself king of the Nobadae and all the Ethiopians and boasts of repeated victories over the Blemmyes, whom he drove from the Nile valley.

sucre.s: Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia, founded by the Spanish in 1538 as La Plata and also called Chuquisaca. From 1559 it was the seat of the Royal Audiencia of Charcas, governing Upper Peru and the silver mines of Potosí, and it had an archbishopric and the…

st-michaels-church-hildesheim.s: St. Michael's Church, Hildesheim, is an early Romanesque abbey church in Lower Saxony built under Bishop Bernward between about 1010 and 1033.

st-michaels-church-schwabisch-hall.s: St. Michael's Church, Schwäbisch Hall, is the main church of the former imperial city of Hall in Württemberg.

siad-barre.s: Siad Barre was a Somali army general who seized power in a coup on 21 October 1969, days after the assassination of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke, and ruled the Somali Democratic Republic until 1991. He proclaimed scientific socialism and introduced a Latin script for…

sirhind.s: Sirhind is a historic town in Punjab, India, on the road between Delhi and Lahore, which was the seat of a Mughal governorship controlling the plains south of the Sutlej. Its governor Wazir Khan executed the two youngest sons of Guru Gobind Singh in 1704, and Banda Singh…

second-french-empire.s: The Second French Empire was the regime of Napoleon III, who as president of the Second Republic seized power in 1851 and proclaimed himself emperor in 1852. It modernised Paris and the economy, expanded French colonies and helped Piedmont-Sardinia against Austria in 1859,…

sanjak-of-smederevo.s: The Sanjak of Smederevo, later known as the Pashalik of Belgrade, was an Ottoman province in central Serbia created after the conquest of Smederevo in 1459 and governed from Belgrade after 1521. In 1801 renegade janissaries, the dahije, seized power there, and their terror…

saadat-ali-khan-i.s: Saadat Ali Khan I, titled Burhan-ul-Mulk, was a Shia noble from Nishapur who became the first Nawab of Awadh. Appointed governor of Awadh by the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in 1722, he made the province largely autonomous and hereditary.

saadatullah-khan-i.s: Saadatullah Khan I was Nawab of the Carnatic from 1710 to 1732, ruling from Arcot. Under him the governorship of the Carnatic, nominally subordinate to the Nizam of Hyderabad, became in effect a hereditary principality.

saba-ibn-abi-al-suud.s: Saba ibn Abi al-Su'ud was a ruler of the Zurayid dynasty of Aden in Yemen. After years of conflict within the family, he defeated his rivals around 1138 and united Aden under a single line.

sabur-al-saqlabi.s: Sabur al-Saqlabi was a Slavic freedman of the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba who took control of the Lower March of al-Andalus, around Mérida, Badajoz and Lisbon, during the collapse of the caliphate after 1009. On his death in 1022 his vizier Abd Allah ibn al-Aftas seized Badajoz…

sacramento-valley.s: The Sacramento Valley is the northern part of California's Central Valley, drained by the Sacramento River. In the 1840s American settlers gathered there around Sutter's Fort, and in June 1846 a group of them began the Bear Flag Revolt against Mexican rule.

sadaikka-thevar.s: Sadaikka Thevar was a Maravar chief who founded the line of the Sethupathis of Ramnad in southern Tamil Nadu. Around 1605 the Madurai Nayaks recognised him as Sethupathi, guardian of the causeway and pilgrimage route to Rameswaram.

sadaqa-ibn-mansur.s: Sadaqa ibn Mansur was the most powerful ruler of the Mazyadid dynasty of central Iraq, an Arab Shia family. Around 1101 he founded al-Hilla on the Euphrates near ancient Babylon, which became the capital of the dynasty and a great centre of Shia learning.

saddam-hussein.s: Saddam Hussein was the Ba'athist ruler of Iraq, effective leader from the 1970s and president from 1979 to 2003. His dictatorship relied on the security services and repression, including the Anfal campaign against the Kurds.

sadri-maqsudi.s: Sadri Maqsudi was a Tatar lawyer and politician who sat in the Russian State Duma and led efforts for Muslim autonomy after the 1917 revolution. He was a leader of the project for an Idel-Ural State in the Volga region.

sadyr-japarov.s: Sadyr Japarov is a Kyrgyz nationalist politician. Released from prison during the unrest after the disputed elections of October 2020, he became prime minister and acting president, then won the presidential election of January 2021.

saeed-bin-maktoum-al-maktoum.s: Saeed bin Maktoum Al Maktoum was ruler of Dubai from 1912 to 1958. During his reign Dubai grew as the main trading port of the Trucial Coast, drawing merchants from Persia, though the collapse of pearling in the 1930s brought hardship.

sahib-ata-fakhr-al-din-ali.s: Sahib Ata Fakhr al-Din Ali was vizier of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum for several decades under Mongol overlordship. A great builder, he founded mosques, madrasas and caravanserais, among them the Sahib Ata complex and the Gök Medrese in Konya and Sivas.

sahl-smbatean.s: Sahl Smbatean was an Armenian prince in Artsakh, in the former lands of Caucasian Albania, in the 9th century. In 837 he captured Babak Khorramdin, leader of a long revolt against the Abbasid caliphate, and handed him over to the caliph's general Afshin, for which he was…

sahle-selassie.s: Sahle Selassie was ruler of Shewa in central Ethiopia from 1813 to 1847, the first of his line to take the title negus, king. He expanded Shewa into Oromo lands, combined Orthodox Christian kingship with alliances with Muslim and Oromo neighbours, and received British and…

said-al-ahwal.s: Sa'id al-Ahwal was a ruler of the Najahid dynasty of Zabid in the Tihama of Yemen, a son of its founder Najah. After the Sulayhids took Zabid, he killed the Sulayhid ruler Ali ibn Muhammad and restored his family's rule.

said-al-dawla.s: Sa'id al-Dawla was the last effective Hamdanid emir of Aleppo, reigning from 991 to 1002. His emirate was squeezed between the Byzantine Empire and the Fatimid caliphate, and he relied on Byzantine help against Fatimid sieges.

said-ali-bin-said-omar.s: Said Ali bin Said Omar was sultan of Bambao on Grande Comore (Ngazidja) in the late 19th century. Backed by the French adventurer Léon Humblot, he made himself paramount sultan of the island and in 1886 signed a treaty placing all of Grande Comore under a French protectorate.

said-bin-hamad-al-qasimi.s: Said bin Hamad Al Qasimi was sheikh of Kalba, a town on the Gulf of Oman coast held by a branch of the Al Qasimi family of Sharjah. In 1936 Britain recognised him as an independent ruler among the Trucial States, in return for permission to build an emergency landing ground…

said-ibn-harun.s: Said ibn Harun was the founder of the taifa of Santa María del Algarve, a small Muslim kingdom around present-day Faro in southern Portugal. Around 1018, as the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart, this member of a local Arab family made himself independent in the coastal town…

said-ibn-idris.s: Said ibn Idris was emir of Nekor, a small Salihid emirate on the Rif coast of northern Morocco, in the 9th century. A grandson of the dynasty's founder Salih ibn Mansur, he built the town of Nekor near modern Al Hoceima as the emirate's capital.

said-bin-sultan.s: Said bin Sultan was sultan of Muscat and Oman from 1806 to 1856, the most powerful ruler of the Omani maritime empire. He extended Omani control along the East African coast, taking Mombasa from the Mazrui in 1837, and moved his court to Zanzibar, where he developed clove…

said-mohamed-cheikh.s: Said Mohamed Cheikh was a Comorian politician who led the islands' government under French rule. When the Territory of the Comoros gained internal autonomy in 1961 he became head of its government council, holding the post until his death in 1970.

said-musa.s: Said Musa is a Belizean lawyer and politician of the People's United Party who served as prime minister of Belize from 1998 to 2008. One of the generation of leaders who followed independence in 1981, he alternated in power with the United Democratic Party.

said-pasha.s: Said Pasha was the Ottoman wali of Egypt from 1854 to 1863, a son of Muhammad Ali. In 1854 he granted his friend Ferdinand de Lesseps the concession to dig the Suez Canal, whose costs later burdened Egyptian finances.

saif-bin-sultan.s: Saif bin Sultan was imam of Oman from 1692 to 1711, the most powerful ruler of the Ya'aruba dynasty. He built up a strong navy, and in 1698 his forces took Fort Jesus at Mombasa from the Portuguese after a long siege, extending Omani influence along the East African coast.

saigo-takamori.s: Saigo Takamori was a samurai of the Satsuma Domain and one of the leaders of the Meiji Restoration of 1868. He commanded imperial forces in the Boshin War, negotiated the peaceful surrender of Edo and arranged lenient terms for defeated domains such as Shonai.

saint-cuthbert.s: Saint Cuthbert was a Northumbrian monk and bishop of Lindisfarne, the most venerated saint of northern England. After Viking raids his community carried his relics to Chester-le-Street and in 995 to Durham, where his shrine became the centre of the cathedral.

saint-emmeram.s: Saint Emmeram was a Frankish bishop who worked as a missionary in Bavaria and was martyred in the 7th century. His tomb at Regensburg became the site of a Benedictine abbey named after him, whose abbots were for long also bishops of Regensburg.

saint-nicholas.s: Saint Nicholas was a 4th-century bishop of Myra in Lycia, in present-day Turkey, venerated across Eastern and Western Christianity as a wonder-worker and patron of sailors and children. In 1087 merchants from Bari carried his relics from Myra to their city, where the Basilica…

saito-dosan.s: Saito Dosan was a Japanese warlord of the Sengoku period who seized control of Mino province from the Toki family, earning the nickname 'viper of Mino'. Later legend made him a former oil merchant, though modern historians think his father began the family's rise.

sajjan-singh-of-ratlam.s: Sajjan Singh was the Rathore maharaja of Ratlam, a princely state in Malwa in central India, from 1893 until 1947. Under British paramountcy he ruled a salute state of the Malwa Agency, and he served as an officer with the British Indian Army in the First World War.

sakai-tadakatsu.s: Sakai Tadakatsu was a daimyo from the Sakai family, one of the most trusted hereditary vassals of the Tokugawa. In 1622 the shogunate moved him to Shonai in Dewa province, on the Sea of Japan coast, with an assessed yield of about 138,000 koku.

sakai-tadashige.s: Sakai Tadashige was the last daimyo of Himeji Domain in Harima province. He served as tairo, the shogun's great elder, at the very end of the Tokugawa shogunate.

sakthan-thampuran.s: Sakthan Thampuran was maharaja of Cochin in Kerala from 1790 to 1805. He curbed the power of the Nair nobles and the landed temple trustees, reorganised the administration and revenue, and encouraged trade by settling merchants.

salah-bey.s: Salah Bey was the Ottoman bey of Constantine, in eastern Algeria, from 1771 to 1792, under the authority of the dey of Algiers. He reformed the administration, built mosques, madrasas and bridges in Constantine and promoted farming in the province.

salih-ibn-mansur.s: Salih ibn Mansur was an Arab of Himyarite descent who founded the Emirate of Nekor on the Rif coast of northern Morocco. Around 710 the Umayyad Caliphate granted him the region, where he preached Islam among the Berber tribes.

salih-ibn-tarif.s: Salih ibn Tarif was the second leader of the Barghawata, a Berber confederation on the Atlantic coast of Morocco. Around 744, after his father Tarif had joined the Berber revolt against the Umayyads, he proclaimed himself a prophet and gave his people a new religion with a…

salim-al-atrash.s: Salim al-Atrash was a Druze leader from the powerful al-Atrash family of the Hauran in southern Syria. When France granted Jabal al-Druze autonomy under its mandate in 1921, he became the first governor of the Jabal Druze State.

salim-bin-abdallah.s: Salim bin Abdallah was a Swahili-Arab trader from the East African coast, linked with Zanzibar, who settled at Nkhotakota on the western shore of Lake Malawi around 1845. Taking the title Jumbe, he founded a trading state that shipped slaves and ivory across the lake towards…

salim-ibn-rashid-al-kharusi.s: Salim ibn Rashid al-Kharusi was an Ibadi imam of Oman, elected by scholars and tribal leaders at Tanuf in 1913 in opposition to the sultan of Muscat and his British ties. His forces took Nizwa and threatened Muscat, which was saved by British Indian troops.

salima-machamba.s: Salima Machamba was the last queen of Mohéli in the Comoros, a descendant of the Merina royal family of Madagascar. She came to the throne as a child under a French protectorate and in 1901 married a French gendarme, moving to France.

salinguerra-ii-torelli.s: Salinguerra II Torelli was the leader of the Ghibelline Torelli family in Ferrara and for decades the city's dominant figure. He fought the Guelph Este marquises for control of the commune and allied himself with Emperor Frederick II.

sam-houston.s: Sam Houston was an American soldier and politician who commanded the Texan army in the Texas Revolution. On 21 April 1836 he defeated and captured Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto, securing Texan independence.

samba-gelaajo-jeegi.s: Samba Gelaajo Jeegi was a prince of the Denianke dynasty of Futa Toro, in the Senegal River valley, who fought for the throne in the 18th century. He became the hero of an epic sung by griots, in which he wins back his inheritance by courage and the help of his companions.

sambor-prei-kuk.s: Sambor Prei Kuk is an archaeological site in Kampong Thom province, Cambodia, identified with Isanapura, capital of the Chenla kingdom under King Isanavarman I in the 7th century. It contains over a hundred brick temples, many octagonal, decorated with carved lintels and reliefs.

samia-suluhu-hassan.s: Samia Suluhu Hassan is a Tanzanian politician from Zanzibar who became the country's first woman president in March 2021. A member of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi, she had served as vice-president from 2015 and succeeded on the death of John Magufuli.

samuel-ajayi-crowther.s: Samuel Ajayi Crowther was a Yoruba linguist and clergyman who was freed from a slave ship as a boy and educated in Sierra Leone. He worked as a missionary at Abeokuta, translated the Bible into Yoruba and led the Church Missionary Society's Niger mission, founding a station at…

samuel-maharero.s: Samuel Maharero was paramount chief of the Herero in German South West Africa, succeeding his father Maharero in 1890. Faced with land loss, debt and abuses by settlers, he led the Herero rising of January 1904.

samuil-buachidze.s: Samuil Buachidze was a Georgian Bolshevik revolutionary who led the Soviet government of the Terek region in the North Caucasus in 1918. As chairman of its council of people's commissars, he tried to balance the land claims of the Terek Cossacks and the mountain peoples.

san-diego.s: San Diego is a port city in southern California, near the border with Mexico. In 1769 the Portolá expedition and Franciscans under Junípero Serra founded a presidio and the first mission of Alta California there.

san-jose-costa-rica.s: San José is the capital and largest city of Costa Rica, in the Central Valley. Founded in the 18th century, it became capital in 1823 after a brief civil war in which its republicans defeated the conservative towns of Cartago and Heredia over joining Mexico.

sancho-garces-i-of-pamplona.s: Sancho Garcés I was king of Pamplona from 905 to 925 and founder of the Jiménez dynasty. He displaced the Íñiguez line, expanded his kingdom south into the Ebro valley and La Rioja, and fought the Banu Qasi and the emirate of Córdoba.

sancho-garcia-of-castile.s: Sancho García was count of Castile from 995 to 1017. He fought Almanzor and his sons and took advantage of the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba, intervening in its civil war in 1009 and recovering frontier fortresses.

sancho-ii-of-castile.s: Sancho II was king of Castile from 1065 to 1072, the eldest son of Ferdinand I, who divided his realms among his children. Aided by his commander Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, he fought his brothers and took León and Galicia.

sancho-vi-william-of-gascony.s: Sancho VI William was duke of Gascony from about 1009 to 1032, the last male ruler of the native ducal line. He had close ties with Sancho III of Pamplona and governed from Bordeaux.

sancho-vii-of-navarre.s: Sancho VII, called the Strong, was king of Navarre from 1194 to 1234. In 1212 he fought with Castile and Aragon at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, a decisive Christian victory over the Almohads, and the chains in Navarre's arms are said to recall it.

sandor-garbai.s: Sándor Garbai was a Hungarian Social Democratic politician who chaired the Revolutionary Governing Council of the Hungarian Soviet Republic in 1919. Formally head of the government, he had less real power than Béla Kun, who controlled foreign affairs.

sang-nila-utama.s: Sang Nila Utama is the legendary founder of the Kingdom of Singapura, known from the Malay Annals. According to the story, this prince of Palembang landed on the island of Temasek, saw a beast he took for a lion and named the place Singapura, the 'lion city', around 1299.

sangram-shah.s: Sangram Shah was a Gond king of Garha-Katanga in central India in the early 16th century. He expanded the kingdom from its base near modern Jabalpur to dozens of forts across the Narmada valley, making it one of the largest states of the region.

sansar-chand-katoch.s: Sansar Chand was the Katoch raja of Kangra in the Himalayan foothills from 1775 to 1823. He recovered Kangra fort from the Mughals and made his kingdom the leading power among the hill states, and his court patronised the Kangra school of painting.

sant-marti-dempuries.s: Sant Martí d'Empúries is a village on the Costa Brava in Catalonia, on what was once a small island at the mouth of the Fluvià. Phocaean Greeks from Massalia set up their first trading post there around 575 BCE, the Palaiapolis of Emporion.

santa-igia.s: Santa Igia was the capital of the medieval Judicate of Cagliari in southern Sardinia, on the edge of the lagoon west of present-day Cagliari. The judges ruled from there with their palace and cathedral from about the 11th century.

sierra-nevada-de-santa-marta.s: The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is an isolated mountain range on the Caribbean coast of northern Colombia, rising to over 5,700 metres, among the highest coastal ranges in the world. It was the home of the Tairona chiefdoms, who built stone-terraced towns such as the Ciudad…

santa-marta.s: Santa Marta is a port city on the Caribbean coast of Colombia, founded by Rodrigo de Bastidas in 1525 and one of the oldest Spanish towns in South America. It served as a base for the conquest of the interior.

santiago-de-liniers.s: Santiago de Liniers was a French-born officer in Spanish service who led the defence of Buenos Aires against the British invasions of 1806 and 1807. His success with local militias made him a popular hero, and he became viceroy of the Río de la Plata from 1807 to 1809.

santiago-marino.s: Santiago Mariño was a Venezuelan independence leader who in 1813 freed eastern Venezuela from Spanish rule while Simón Bolívar campaigned in the west. He shared power uneasily with Bolívar in the Second Republic, which fell to royalist forces under José Tomás Boves in 1814.

sao-hkun-hseng.s: Sao Hkun Hseng was saopha, or prince, of Hsipaw, a northern Shan state in Burma, from 1886. Coming to power as the British annexed Upper Burma, he cooperated with the new rulers and became one of the most important Shan chiefs under British protection.

sao-kya-seng.s: Sao Kya Seng was the last saopha of Hsipaw, a Shan state in Burma, educated as a mining engineer in the United States, where he met his Austrian wife Inge Sargent. He introduced land reforms and sat in the Burmese parliament.

sarah-wescot-williams.s: Sarah Wescot-Williams is a politician from Sint Maarten who became its first prime minister on 10 October 2010, when the island became an autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands after the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles. She had earlier led the…

saruhan-bey.s: Saruhan Bey was a Turkmen commander who founded the beylik of Saruhan in western Anatolia. In 1313 he took Magnesia, modern Manisa, from the Byzantines and made it his capital in the Hermus valley.

sarvajna-singabhupala.s: Sarvajna Singabhupala was a ruler of the Recherla Nayaka (Velama) dynasty of Rachakonda in Telangana in the 14th century. A noted patron and scholar, he wrote the Rasarnava Sudhakara, a Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and poetics still studied today.

satake-yoshiatsu.s: Satake Yoshiatsu, known by the art name Shozan, was daimyo of Kubota Domain in Akita from 1758 to 1785. Interested in Western learning, he invited Hiraga Gennai to advise on the domain's mines.

satake-yoshishige.s: Satake Yoshishige was a Sengoku-period warlord who led the Satake clan of Hitachi province. Nicknamed the 'demon of Hitachi', he fought the Later Hojo for control of the northern Kanto and formed alliances with neighbouring lords against them.
